justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable baseline with a mild upward drift across time horizons. The 1-day estimate of 65.9 is anchored primarily to the most recent observed value or momentum in the series, assuming no major shock occurs overnight. The slight increase to 66.1 at one week and 66.5 at one month reflects a gentle positive trend I detected in the underlying data, whether from gradual structural drift, seasonal patterns, or mean-reversion dynamics pulling the series modestly higher from its current level. The incremental nature of the increases suggests I did not expect a dramatic directional move but did see marginal evidence favoring upside continuation.

The confidence interval widths grow systematically with the forecast horizon, which is a standard feature of forecasting under uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3.4 units, reflecting the typical short-term noise and intraday or overnight variability in the series. By one week, this expands to about 6.6 units, incorporating the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of modest trend reversals. At one month, the interval widens to 12 units, reflecting compounding uncertainty from multiple weekly cycles, potential regime shifts, and the general difficulty of pinning down medium-term outcomes. The relatively symmetric intervals around the point estimates suggest I did not see strong skew risks in either direction at the time of forecasting.

Several risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a positive catalyst such as a strong data release, favorable policy announcement, or momentum breakout could drive the series well above 72.5 within a month. On the downside, an external shock, deteriorating macro conditions, or a technical breakdown could push values below 60.5. Even at the one-day horizon, a surprise event occurring after market close or during off-hours could easily breach the 64.2 to 67.6 range, since such intervals assume roughly normal background volatility rather than fat-tail events.

It is also worth noting that model uncertainty itself is a source of risk not fully captured in these intervals. If the underlying data-generating process has recently shifted in ways not reflected in my training window or the features I weighted, my point estimates could be systematically biased rather than simply noisy. Structural breaks, changes in measurement methodology, or correlated external variables I did not account for all represent ways the true outcome could fall outside my stated confidence bands more frequently than the 10% residual probability I assigned to those tails.
